identification.bodyShape: Robust, elongated jack body, deeper and more compressed than the closely related banded rudderfish, with a forked tail.
identificationTraits: Dark amber-brown stripe runs from the nose through the eye to the front of the first dorsal fin, becoming more pronounced when the fish is excited or feeding.
First dorsal fin has 7 spines, versus 8 in banded rudderfish.
Upper jaw bone curves upward toward the eye.
An amber horizontal stripe runs along the mid-body in some fish, giving the species its common name.
Juveniles show 5–6 dark vertical bars on a yellowish body.
identification.coloration: Brownish or bluish-gray back with a silvery-white belly, plus the diagnostic dark eye stripe and, in some fish, an amber body stripe.
identification.juvenileAppearance: Yellow body with five or six dark vertical bars; schools pelagically around drifting Sargassum mats before settling to demersal habitat at roughly 5–6 months of age.
identification.adultAppearance: Brownish-gray to bluish-gray above and silvery-white below, with the dark eye stripe running from snout through the eye to the first dorsal fin, most vivid when the fish is excited or feeding.

similarSpecies.name: Banded rudderfish (Seriola zonata)
similarSpecies.distinction: Banded rudderfish lacks greater amberjack's dark eye stripe, shows a bluish sheen with a white-tipped tail and first dorsal fin, and has 8 first-dorsal spines versus amberjack's 7.

similarSpecies.name: Almaco jack (Seriola rivoliana)
similarSpecies.distinction: Almaco jack shares the dark eye stripe but has a notably rounder body and elongated soft dorsal rays more than double the length of the rest of that fin; greater amberjack's dorsal fin is more uniform in height.

identification.averageAdultLength: Not separately sourced from typical angling weight; see commonAnglingSize.
identification.typicalWeight: Most commonly up to about 40 lb.
identification.maximumDocumentedSize: Up to about 6 ft and occasionally over 200 lb; females reach larger sizes and greater longevity than males.
identification.longevity: Documented to about 17 years; matures at 3–4 years of age.

social.byLifeStage: Juveniles school strongly around pelagic Sargassum mats; schooling behavior decreases as the fish matures, and adults are comparatively solitary, congregating around specific structure rather than schooling in open water.
social.note: Adult aggregation around a wreck or reef is a structure response, not a schooling behavior in the open-water sense.

feedingStrategy.note: Adults take crabs, squid, and other reef-associated fishes around structure; juveniles feed on zooplankton, including crustacean larvae, in the pelagic Sargassum community.

dielTendency.note: Diel activity pattern was not directly sourced for wild fish; classified as mixed pending a source-backed determination rather than left blank, since the field is required.

behavior.territoriality: Adults hold on specific reef, rock, or wreck structure rather than ranging widely in open water; not documented as aggressively territorial in sourced material.
behavior.coverUse: Structure-oriented as adults — reefs, rocky outcrops, and shipwrecks; juveniles use pelagic Sargassum as cover in open water.
behavior.openWaterBehavior: Juveniles are pelagic, schooling around drifting Sargassum mats before transitioning to demersal, structure-oriented habitat around 5–6 months of age.
behavior.spawningBehavior: Broadcast spawner; adults congregate on reef and wreck structure to spawn, with a spawning peak in spring reported for Gulf and South Atlantic populations, and a single female releasing tens of millions of eggs across a season. This record excludes aggregation sites and precise timing; spawning is conservation context, related to why Gulf harvest is currently restricted under a rebuilding plan, and is not a targeting cue.

diet.primaryNote: Adults are opportunistic structure-associated predators taking crabs, squid, and other fishes around reefs and wrecks; juveniles feed on zooplankton, including crustacean larvae, while pelagic around Sargassum. Diet capacity is not evidence of a current bait event.

lifeStageDiet.youngOfYear: Zooplankton, crustacean larvae, and other small invertebrates in the pelagic Sargassum community.

seasonal_calendar.overview: Greater amberjack shift from pelagic, Sargassum-associated juveniles to structure-holding nearshore/offshore adults. Spring is the reported spawning peak and is conservation context only. Current harvest availability depends heavily on in-season quota status, especially in the Gulf, and is not itself a behavior signal — this calendar describes habitat and structure use, not a fishing season.
